learning.title: A red-proof or a grep only counts if you know what it measured
learning.trigger: A builder, QA or reviewer mutates code to prove a test fails, or greps a branch to confirm or refute someone's report.
learning.mistake: A mutation that never applied left the test green, and the green was read as a weak test. A literal counted once was present in a second place, so the mutant changed only one copy. A value was edited without reading the container around it, so the edit sat in a comment or an unused branch. On #571 a grep of the branch for the symbols a fix introduced (isZodSchema, freezeDeep) found nothing, and the empty result was read as an unverifiable claim. The branch predated the fix, so the absence was the bug the report described.
learning.rule: 1. Assert the mutation applied (git diff shows it) before reading any result. 2. Count the literal you mutate across the tree; mutate every copy or say which one. 3. Read the container shape around the value, not just the value. 4. When a red-proof comes back green, suspect the mutation before the test. 5. When a measurement appears to refute a report, ask which tree it was taken from before believing it: grepping a branch for the symbols a fix introduces returns nothing precisely because the branch predates the fix, so the absence is the finding. A result that agrees with you can still be measuring the wrong tree; state what the result would look like if the report were true, and check that.

verification.requirement: Every red-proof in a PR comment names the git diff line that shows the mutation applied.
Every refuting measurement names the commit it was taken from and the merge base it is compared with.
